purpose: Defensive early-warning model for detecting staged or synchronized activation of TSPU-like or Russian-origin DPI/SORM filtering outside the normal Russian domestic censorship perimeter.
rule: No single indicator is sufficient for attribution. Escalation requires independent signals from different measurement layers.

signals: Simultaneous appearance of protocol-specific blocking for QUIC/TLS/DNS that matches a known TSPU fingerprint rather than generic packet loss.
Consistent TTL/hop localization of injected resets, DNS rewriting, drops or policy responses at the same AS or border segment.
Sudden blocking of DoH/DoT or interception of plaintext DNS to public resolvers while matched TCP/alternate-path controls behave differently.
Cross-provider appearance of the same domain/SNI policy with closely matching timing and packet behavior.
Unexpected foreign-origin traffic begins transiting a Russian or Russian-linked AS that was absent from the stable baseline.
BGP origin or AS-path changes coincide with newly observed filtering or blackholing.
RPKI-invalid or newly originated routes appear for prefixes serving major US cloud/CDN/SaaS endpoints.
Matched bypass paths avoiding the suspected AS do not reproduce the filtering.
Multiple countries with documented Russian DPI/SORM deployments show the same new filtering behavior within a narrow time window.
Changes appear first in networks with known Russian vendor relationships and later in adjacent networks.
OONI/RIPE Atlas measurements show the anomaly clustering by operator or equipment lineage rather than by destination service alone.
Coordinated maintenance/firmware/configuration windows across foreign operators using the same Russian vendor stack.
New procurement, regulator mandates or lawful-interception/filtering requirements appear shortly before behavioral changes.
Public documentation reveals remote-management or vendor-maintained control channels for deployed DPI/SORM equipment.
Users in multiple foreign networks simultaneously lose or degrade access specifically to US-hosted cloud, communications, financial, developer or media services while local services remain normal.
US providers observe geographically clustered reachability changes from ASes with documented Russian-origin filtering equipment.
Traffic from affected countries shifts toward unexpected transit ASes before the service degradation begins.
US-side telemetry sees abrupt protocol mix changes, QUIC collapse, DNS resolver migration, reset bursts or path inflation limited to the affected networks.

escalation_logic.YELLOW: 4-7 points with at least two independent groups: anomalous behavior; freeze baseline and intensify measurements.
escalation_logic.ORANGE: 8-11 points with PACKET_AND_PROTOCOL or ROUTING evidence plus one independent geography/vendor signal: plausible coordinated activation; notify defensive stakeholders and preserve packet/route evidence.
escalation_logic.RED: 12+ points with reproducible path-specific filtering from foreign vantage points, matched bypass controls, and independent replication: strong evidence of coordinated external filtering activity. Attribution to TSPU still requires device/operator linkage.

required_measurements: RIPE Atlas traceroute and DNS measurements from affected and control networks.
RIPE RIS/RouteViews/BGPStream path history and RPKI validation.
Packet captures from consenting/controlled endpoints where lawful.
Matched alternate-path or VPN controls that change routing without changing destination.
US-provider status/RCA data to exclude provider-local incidents.
anti_false_positive_rules: Cloud/provider RCA identifying an internal failure overrides external attribution unless independent network evidence remains unexplained.
A single-country government shutdown is not evidence of Russian remote activation.
Generic latency, packet loss or DNS failure without a stable fingerprint is insufficient.
Commercial Russian vendor presence is a risk factor, not an activation event.
Temporal coincidence alone contributes zero attribution points.
